Guide: Ownership and borrowing

A long, friendly guide to how Drachm frees memory without a garbage collector, what moves, copies and borrows mean, and how to read and fix the compiler's errors.

This guide is for people who have written Python, JavaScript, Java or C, and have never used a language with an ownership system. It assumes nothing beyond the first nine lessons. Read it top to bottom once; afterwards the reference pages are the place to look things up.

Every program and every error message on this page comes from the real compiler. The programs that run have a block labelled "output"; the ones that fail show what drachm check prints.

1. The problem: who frees the memory?

A program needs memory for things whose size is not known in advance: the text of a string, the items of a list. That memory has to be handed back when the program is done with it, or the computer runs out. Someone has to decide when "done" is. Languages answer this in three ways.

You do it by hand (C). You ask for memory with malloc and give it back with free. Nothing checks that you did it right, and three mistakes are easy to make:

Leave out the free and you have a leak: the memory is never returned, and a long-running program slowly eats the machine. Use after free and double free are worse. They corrupt memory, and the program may crash far from the bug, or carry on and do something an attacker chose. A large share of security holes in C and C++ programs are exactly these mistakes.

A garbage collector does it for you (Python, JavaScript, Java). The runtime tracks which values can still be reached and frees the rest. This is safe and easy, and the price is paid while the program runs: the collector needs CPU time and extra memory, it may pause your program at moments you do not choose, and you cannot say exactly when a value is destroyed (which makes it awkward to close a file or release a lock "right when I am done").

The compiler does it for you (Drachm). Drachm has no garbage collector and no free. Instead the compiler follows two ideas:

  1. Every value has exactly one owner, and the value is destroyed when its owner goes out of scope.
  2. Anything else that wants to use the value must borrow it, and the compiler checks that no borrow can outlive the value or get in the way of a change.

The compiler proves this by reading your program, before it runs. The finished program contains the free calls in the right places, exactly as if you had written them correctly in C, and nothing is checked while it runs. Double free and use after free cannot be written in ordinary code, and an owned value is never forgotten. A program that tries is rejected with an error that points at the line.

That is the whole trade. You learn a few rules and the compiler sometimes says no; in return you get C's speed with a garbage collector's safety. The rest of this guide is those rules, one idea at a time.

2. Ownership

One owner, and scope ends

A string owns its text. When the name that owns it goes out of scope (reaches the } of the block it was declared in), the text is freed. A struct can run its own code at that moment with a method called drop, which makes the moment visible:

a is created and owns a Guard.

b lives only inside the if. At its closing brace b is dropped, so "drop b" prints before "end of main".

At the end of main the remaining values are dropped in the reverse order they were made: c first, then a. Reverse order means something made later, which may depend on something made earlier, goes away first.

You never write the cleanup. It happens at the }, every time, even when the function leaves early with return or break.

Moving

If every value has one owner, what does string b = a; mean? It cannot make two owners. It moves the value: b is now the owner and a has nothing.

Nothing is copied by a move. The text stays where it is; only the name that owns it changes. That is why moves are cheap, and why passing a string to a function, returning it, or storing it in a struct are all moves too.

Using a after the move would mean using a value it no longer owns, so the compiler refuses:

The three parts to read in that message are the line where the value moved, the line where you used it, and the help line, which offers the usual fix. With copy the program works:

Copying

The fix is copy. It makes a second, separate value with its own memory:

Copying a long string takes time and memory, so Drachm never does it behind your back: there are no hidden copies. Wherever a copy happens, you wrote copy, and you can search for it.

Values that copy by themselves

Some values are so small that copying is as cheap as moving, and they would be annoying to track. Numbers, bools, and structs made only of such things copy automatically, with no copy needed. The exact rule:

  • Numbers and bools always copy.
  • A struct copies automatically when all its fields copy and its size in memory, padding included, is at most 32 bytes.
  • Everything else moves: strings, structs holding strings, structs bigger than 32 bytes.

The size includes padding the compiler adds between fields, so rearranging fields can change the size, and with it whether a struct is plain-copy. A struct that must never copy by itself, however small, says stays after its name, and then copying it is always explicit:

The compiler's errors line up with this. Moving the 40-byte Big and then reading big.a is an error, and so is moving the stays struct Handle:

Taking one field out

A struct owns its fields, so moving a field out leaves a hole in the struct. Drachm makes you say so with take. A plain string n = p.name; is an error (E0324) that suggests take p.name or copy p.name:

take p.name moves the field out and leaves it empty until you give it a new value; the compiler tracks that for you and rejects any read of an empty field. take p.title leaving "none" moves the old value out and puts a new one in during the same statement, so the field is never empty:

Writing to a field needs permission too (a mut binding or a mut field; see section 5). A struct with a drop() method has to stay complete so it can be dropped properly, so plain take on it is an error and only take x.f leaving v is allowed. Moves and copies has the full rules, and lesson 8 practises them.

3. Borrowing

Looking and changing

Moving everything would be unbearable. A function that only wants to print a string should not have to take it away from you. A borrow lets code use a value without owning it:

  • &T is a shared borrow: it may read.
  • &mut T is a unique borrow: it may read and change.

The borrow is written at the call as well as in the parameter, so you can see in deposit(&mut acc, 20) that acc may change. Inside the function a borrow works like the value itself: reads are automatic (a.balance) and an assignment writes through to the owner's value.

When a function that holds a &mut wants to pass it on and keep using it, it writes lend. Passing it without lend would hand the borrow over (a &mut moves, like a string) and the function could not use it again.

A & borrow is just permission to look, so it copies freely; a &mut moves unless you lend it. Borrowing needs no memory and no copying: it is a pointer the compiler has checked.

Many readers or one writer

Here is the rule the compiler enforces, and it is the heart of the system. At any moment, a value has

  • any number of & borrows, or
  • exactly one &mut borrow,

and never both. People call it "shared XOR mutable". It sounds fussy, so here is what it prevents.

A reader whose data moves. A string stores its text in a block of memory. When it grows past the block, the text is copied to a bigger block and the old one is freed. A &string that points at the old block would now read freed memory:

In C or C++ this is the classic "iterator invalidation" bug (holding a pointer into a vector, then pushing to it). Drachm refuses to compile it, because changing name while first will still be used breaks the rule:

Two writers. If two names can both change one value, neither can rely on what it sees. A function that checks p.hp > 0 and then subtracts may find that the other writer changed it in between. The compiler (and a reader of the code) can assume that a &mut is alone, which also lets it generate faster code. Two &mut at once is E0303, shown in section 6.

Calls that look like they break the rule

A method call borrows its receiver, so b::add(b::size()) seems to borrow b twice, once to read and once to change. It is fine, because the borrow for the change only starts when the call itself runs, and by then b::size() has finished and handed back a plain number. This is called a two-phase borrow. What is not fine is an argument that is still holding a borrow when the change starts:

b::first() gives back a borrow of text inside b, and put is going to change b while that borrow is still alive. The first three lines of the last program are fine because size() returns a number, and s::len()->text() makes a new string.

4. How long a borrow lives

A borrow ends at its last use

A borrow does not last until the end of the block. It lasts until its last use. The compiler looks at your program as a graph of what runs after what, and asks, for every borrow, "is it used again from here?". If not, the borrow is over and the value is free to change again.

This is why the programs you write usually need no extra braces or tricks to satisfy the borrow rules. Hold a borrow only as long as you need it. It also means the order of your lines matters, and many borrow errors are fixed by moving the use up.

Which parameter does the result come from?

A function can return a borrow, as name_of does in the lesson. The caller must then keep the thing it points into safe, so the compiler needs to know which argument the result borrows from. Most of the time it reads the body and works that out itself. You write lives only when it is ambiguous.

Reading it top to bottom:

  • first_word has one borrowed parameter, so the result can only come from text. Nothing to write.
  • longer could return a or b, so it says lives a, b. The caller keeps both alive while it uses the result. Without that, the error is E0308, and its help line is the fix.
  • struct Reader lives src has a borrowed field, so the struct says which field borrows. A Reader is only valid while the string it points at is.
  • A method names self with lives from, joining sources with or: lives from self or key.

lives names whole parameters, never parts of them, and listing more than the body needs is allowed (a caller just keeps more things alive). Here is the error without it:

Because lives a, b keeps both arguments borrowed for as long as the result is used, changing either of them in that time is an error. That follows directly from the rule, and it is pitfall 6 below.

See Where a borrow comes from for the other lives errors (E0309, E0320) and for the limits of what it tracks.

5. Mutability

Ownership says who frees a value. Mutability says who may change it, and Drachm makes you spell it out. By default a binding keeps the value it was given. Three words change that:

WordOn aWhat it allows
mutbindinggive the name a new value, and change its contents
openbindingchange the contents (fields, +=, lending &mut), never reassign
mutfieldchange that field on a struct you own, even through a plain binding

open also lets you declare a binding without a value and give it its one value later (open string xs;), and write open parameters (none fill(open string s)).

Look at what the compiler says when you forget. A plain binding cannot be given a new value, and cannot be lent as &mut:

Methods and mut fields

You do not mark methods as changing or not. The compiler reads the body: a method changes self if it writes to self or calls a method that does. That gives three kinds of method:

  • reads only. Works on any value, through & or &mut.
  • changes only mut fields (like hit above). Works on a value you own even when the binding is not mut; not through a &; fine through &mut.
  • changes anything else. Needs a mut or open binding (E0312) or a &mut.

A mut field is a convenience for things like counters on values you own. It is not a way around the borrow rules: through a & borrow nothing changes, not even a mut field. If you want to change something you need to hold &mut, because code that only looks cannot also change.

There is no method that consumes self: methods only borrow it. To hand back a field of a borrowed self, return a copy (return copy self.name;), because the compiler will not guess that you meant one.

6. How the compiler checks it, and how to read its errors

What happens to your program

You do not need this to use the language, but it helps explain the messages. After type checking, the compiler turns each function into MIR, a small flat program of numbered steps with the control flow made explicit. Then two passes read it:

  1. Moves analysis follows every path through the function and records, at each step, which names still own a value. This is how it knows a is empty after string b = a;, even if the move happened in only one branch of an if or in the previous trip round a loop, and where to put the drops.
  2. The borrow checker records every borrow as a loan ("&name made at step 3") and works out the steps where it is still needed. Then it checks every step that moves, drops or changes something against the loans in force there.

drachm check --dump-mir file.drh prints the MIR of the E0302 program below. Here is its heart (the _2 = &_1 line is the borrow, and Drop(_1) followed by _1 = const "Sam" is the change):

The Drop happens while the loan is still in use, and that is the error. The same check runs the same way for every program, so the messages are consistent. --dump-borrowck shows the loans and the steps they cover.

Reading an error

Every borrow error has the same four parts. Here is E0302:

  1. The code and headline. E0302: cannot change name while it is borrowed. drachm explain E0302 says more, and the error index lists every code.
  2. The location, main.drh:6:5: file, line, column of the ^^^^ mark.
  3. The labelled lines. Each marked line plays a role: the borrow was made here, the change is attempted here, and the borrow is still used here. The error is the sandwich: the first and last bracket a stretch of the program in which the middle thing is not allowed.
  4. help. Usually the fix, written for this program.

Read the labels in line order and you can usually tell the story: "I borrowed name, then I changed it, then I tried to use the borrow".

E0301 to E0307

The moves and the borrows each have their own code. Here they are, in order, each with the smallest program that makes it. E0301 you have already met above (E0301 in section 2): a value is used after it moved. It is also the error when a value moves inside a loop and the next trip round uses it, or when it moved on only some paths.

E0302: change while borrowed. Shown above. The fix is to finish with the borrow first, or to borrow again later.

E0303: two &mut at once. A second &mut to p is made while the first is still going to be used:

Use the first borrow up before making the second, or use one borrow for both calls.

E0304: using a value while it is &mut borrowed. While a unique borrow is going to be used, even reading the owner is unsafe, because the borrow may be mid-change:

Read through the borrow, as the help line says. This one runs:

E0305: moving a value that is borrowed. The borrower would be left pointing at a value that now lives somewhere else:

Finish with first before the move, or hand over a copy.

E0306: a borrow that outlives its value. local is dropped at the end of its block, but keep is used after it:

The help line is the fix: make the value live as long as the borrow. This is "use after free", caught at compile time:

E0307: returning a borrow of a local. A function's own values die when it returns, so a borrow of one would dangle:

Return the string itself (return s;), which moves it to the caller:

7. Common pitfalls and their fixes

Each pitfall is a short program that fails, the real error, and a version that works.

1. Using a value after it moved into a call

Passing name to greet(string s) hands the text over. The second call has nothing left:

If greet only needs to look, make the parameter a borrow. This is nearly always better than copy:

Use greet(copy name) when the function really needs its own string, for example to store it.

2. Moving a field out of a struct

You met this in section 2: string n = p.name; is E0324. The fixes are copy p.name if both places need the text, or take p.name (with leaving to keep the struct tidy) if the struct no longer does.

3. Returning a borrow of something local

A parameter taken by value is a local variable of the function. Returning a borrow of it is E0307 too:

Take the parameter as a borrow, so the caller keeps owning it and the function can hand back a borrow into the caller's value:

Or return an owned value (return copy p.name;) and change the return type to string.

4. Changing something while it is borrowed

Two shapes of this are worth knowing. Growing a string with += counts as a change, exactly like assigning to it (you saw it in section 3). The same holds for a field: n.text is borrowed, so n.text += "!" is a change.

The fix is to finish with first before the change, or to not hold the borrow:

The other shape is the two-phase one from section 3: b::put(b::first()) changes b while the argument still borrows it. Pass a number or a copy instead of a borrow of the same value.

5. Borrowing in a loop

A borrow made before a loop and used inside it is "still going to be used" on every trip round, so a change inside the loop breaks it, even though the use comes before the change in the text:

Make the borrow inside the loop, so each trip round has a new one that ends before the change:

6. Holding a borrow longer than you meant

A function that returns a borrow ties the result to its arguments. With lives a, b the result r keeps both x and y borrowed for as long as r is used:

You are not using y in a clever way here; you are changing something that r may still point into. Use r first:

A struct is conservative in the same way. The compiler does not track which part of a parameter a result points at, so after &string r = rest(&p); the whole of p is borrowed while r is used:

When that is too strict, finish with the borrow first, or copy what you need out (string r = copy p.src;).

7. A copy that does nothing

copy is for values that would otherwise move. On a number it has nothing to do, so the compiler warns (W0322). It is a warning, not an error, and your program still builds:

Remove the copy, as the help says (uint32 m = n;). The warning exists because a stray copy makes a reader wonder what is being protected. A setting to switch this lint off is part of the planned project config; it does not exist yet.

8. Passing m when the function wants &m

The call must show what the callee may do. Passing the value itself where a borrow is expected is E0321, and the help line is the exact call to write:

Write shout(&mut word) and show(&word). The &mut also needs word to be mut or open (E0312). Two related mistakes:

  • Passing a &mut you hold on to a second function moves it, so the next use is E0301. Write lend s:
  • Passing a &mut you hold where a & is wanted needs &s, which lends a shared view for the call. A bare show(s) is E0330:

Both fixes in one program that runs:

9. A struct that holds a borrow, without lives

A field of type &string means the struct is only valid while something else is. The struct has to say so:

If the struct could simply own its text, a string field avoids the whole question. Prefer owning fields unless you are avoiding a big copy.

8. The escape hatch: unsafe

The checks are conservative. They only accept programs they can prove safe, so a few correct programs get rejected, and a few jobs (talking to hardware, writing your own data structure, calling C) cannot be proved at all. For those, Drachm has raw pointers, and the compiler takes its hands off.

Using them needs two things, so nobody uses them by accident: the line //--!$unsafe: true at the top of the file, and an unsafe { } block around each operation on a pointer. *T is a pointer you can write through, and address of n makes one from a mut or open binding. Making, reading and writing through a pointer all go inside unsafe { }. address of an immutable binding gives a *fixed T, which can only be read.

Inside the block you promise that the pointer is valid and that nothing else is changing the value. Break that promise and you have C's bugs back: nothing checks a raw pointer for use after free. Raw pointers also move like strings, and there is no *mut: one pointer kind, *T.

You will rarely need any of this. Strings, structs, borrows and lives cover ordinary programs, and the rules in this guide are what keep them safe. Keep unsafe blocks small and wrap them in a function with a safe signature, so the promise is made in one place. Unsafe and pointers has the rest, including freeze, thaw and unsafe functions.

9. If you know Rust or C++

Drachm's ideas will look familiar if you have used Rust, and its goals overlap with C++'s. The rules are close in places and different in others, and the syntax is its own. A factual comparison:

DrachmRustC++
Assigning a stringmovesmovescopies
Which types copy by themselvesnumbers, bools, structs of those up to 32 bytes; stays opts outtypes that implement Copyalmost everything
Making a copycopy x, always writtenx.clone()implicit, or written
Borrow at the callf(&x), f(&mut x)f(&x), f(&mut x)f(x); the reference is only in the signature
Passing a &mut onlend simplicit reborrownot applicable
Taking a field outtake p.f, take p.f leaving vpartial move, or mem::take / mem::replacestd::move(p.f)
Who can change a valuemut, open, mut fieldsmut, interior types (Cell, RefCell)const and mutable
Does a method change selfinferred from the bodydeclared (&self / &mut self)declared (const)
Method that consumes selfnone: methods only borrowyes (self)no (moving is by hand)
Lifetimesinferred; lives names whole parameters when ambiguous'a parameters, with elision rulesnone; the compiler does not check
How long a borrow livesuntil its last useuntil its last usenot checked
Cleanupscope end; drop(); destroy x; to run it earlyscope end; Drop; drop(x)destructors
Opting outunsafe plus a file flag; *T, *fixed Tunsafe; *const T, *mut Teverything is allowed
Runtime cost of the checksnone, all at compile timenonenone (nothing is checked)

The differences that matter day to day: copies are always written and there are no hidden ones; a field leaves a struct only through take; lend replaces silent reborrowing so you can see where a &mut goes; methods need no annotation to say whether they change self; and the keywords are English words rather than sigils and apostrophes.
